units: two neighboring homes show opposite characters
the older one has thick stone walls and few openings
the newer one offers wide glazed surfaces on a light frame
the old building holds its coolness better when the air is hot
the recent building follows outdoor temperature swings quickly
the occupants of the old home report a coating that soaks up water rising from the ground
a waterproof layer was laid under the outer cladding of the recent home
the occupants of the recent home worry when air renewal stops
a building tradesman holds that each construction answers a different purpose
text: Two homes sit side by side along the same road, and you tell them apart at a glance. The older one squats behind thick stone walls, under a low roof, with hardly any openings. The newer one stands taller, lining up wide panes of glass across a frame of pale timber. When the air turns hot, the old walls keep their coolness and warm up slowly. The recent one tracks whatever the outdoors does and answers the smallest shift. People in the older home complain that the render drinks up damp rising from the ground. Their neighbors praise the sealed layer laid under their cladding, yet they worry about stale air whenever the ventilation stops. A tradesman who works on both kinds refuses to pick a winner. One was raised to stand for ages without upkeep, the other to burn far less energy.

units: the writer holds that fast building work spoils the look of the streets
he regrets that heavy hand-worked materials give way to light elements
he notes the loss of homes with irregular shapes
those irregular shapes came from crooked plots or from split inheritances
buildings put up now repeat matching volumes stacked without hesitation
the size of a home was once judged by its extra spaces such as attics and cellars
it is now judged by the room count that is advertised
the writer refuses to call for a return to the past
he asks that a building be judged on what it will offer the next generation
text: Building at speed has become a habit, and the habit is making our streets poorer. Consider the losses one by one. Materials first: the heavy block, worked by chisel and by a patient hand, gives way to lightweight panels that no palm has ever touched. Shape next: the odd-angled dwellings, born of a crooked plot or of an inheritance split among heirs, vanish behind matching volumes that get stacked without a second thought. Use, last of all: a roomy home once meant nooks, an attic under the beams, a cellar below the boards. Now it means a room count printed in a listing. I am not asking anyone to turn back, and I distrust easy longing for what is gone. I ask only that a building be measured by what it will hand to the generation after us, and not by how quickly the site was finished.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman started out sorting beams on a renovation job
he was learning to tell sound timber from a piece ruined by damp
he then joined a workshop that put wood together without glue or metal parts
there he took up layout, cutting and fitting against irregular walls
a fall from scaffolding kept him off building sites while he healed
during that break he drew roof frames for other crews
on his return he opened his own workshop and took on two apprentices
he teaches that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan sent from afar
text: The carpenter started out as an apprentice on a renovation job, where sorting the beams fell to him. He had to tell rough but sound timber from a crumbling piece that damp had eaten through. After a few seasons he moved to a workshop that cut its joints by hand, using neither glue nor metal fasteners. There he picked up layout, full-scale drawing, angled cuts, and at last the fitting of pieces against walls that never stood true. A fall from scaffolding kept him off sites through a long recovery, and he filled the break by drawing roof frames for other crews. When he came back he opened a workshop of his own and took on two apprentices. He tells them again and again that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan mailed in, because an old wall keeps moving and no frontage runs plumb.

units: cracks ran through the building from its base to its top
a broken gutter had soaked the foundations over a long period
the water seeping in had dissolved the mortar and shifted the stones
the staircase had lost its steadiness
the site manager put the cause right before the appearance
he drained the foot of the wall, made the binders good and changed the worn steps
that order of work explains the soundness gained and the plainness of the result
some visitors find the result disappointing for want of a visible effect
the writer faults the uniform windows that wipe out the trace of older openings
the writer still holds the choice defensible because a finish laid over shifting walls would have split
text: What this restoration deserves credit for is largely what it refused to do. Cracks ran through the building from footing to ridge, because a broken gutter had been soaking the foundations for season upon season. Water seeping in dissolved the mortar, stones slid out of line, and the staircase turned wobbly underfoot. So the site manager went after the cause before the appearance. He drained the foot of the wall, made the binders good again, and swapped out the worn treads. That order of work explains why the structure now stands sound. It also explains how plain the outcome looks, plain enough that some visitors leave disappointed for want of anything to admire. The windows are too uniform, and they wipe out the record of older openings. Still the choice holds up: any finish laid over shifting walls would have split.

units: the writer lives above a former workshop
the floor creaked under every step and disturbed the neighbor below
shims, screws and thick rugs had settled nothing
a joiner found the source of the noise in a single visit
the joists were resting on a sagging beam
the hollow under the floor made every footfall louder
the joiner put a sturdy prop in the cellar and fixed the boards down again
the noise stopped that same evening
the neighbor and the writer made peace after the repair
text: I finally have a quiet moment, so here is how the floorboard saga ended. Ever since I moved into this apartment above a former workshop, every step set the boards creaking and woke my downstairs neighbor. Shims, screws, carpets thick enough to trip over: nothing improved matters. Then a joiner came up to look and identified the reason during a single visit. The joists were resting on a beam that had sagged, and the hollow underneath turned every footfall into a drum. He wedged a sturdy prop into the cellar and refastened the boards onto fresh battens. By that evening the apartment had gone completely quiet. My neighbor brought me a potted plant to celebrate, and we laughed about two miserable seasons spent resenting each other. Come and stay soon, the spare room is ready.

units: heating costs come from what the walls are made of and not from the age of the building
a thick wall stores heat and gives it back through the night
a light partition loses its heat as soon as the heating stops
insulation works differently on an old wall and on a recent one
an old wall has to let vapor through or water builds up inside its thickness
a recent wall needs an unbroken barrier and controlled air renewal
tradesmen advise picking what you can mend yourself
render is patched with a mason's tool
a panel made in a factory has to be swapped out whole
text: So does an old house cost more to heat than a recent one? Mostly it depends on what the walls are made of, not on the age of the building. A thick wall absorbs heat and releases it overnight, whereas a thin partition surrenders everything the minute the boiler shuts off. And insulation, what does that change? Enormously, though not in the same manner on either side. On an old wall the vapor has to pass straight through, otherwise water accumulates inside the thickness and the wall deteriorates. On a recent wall you want the opposite: an unbroken barrier, plus air renewal kept under control. So which should you choose? Whichever you can repair yourself, the tradesmen answer. Render you patch with a trowel. A panel assembled in a factory you replace in one piece, or not at all.

units: the site manager set out the renovation plan to the local residents
he sorted his answers around three worries
knocking down the partitions will take two weeks and the loud machines will stop in late afternoon
a fine sheet will wrap the scaffolding to hold down the dust
the rubble will be wetted before it is carried out
the sidewalk will be routed around the work but the ground-floor shop will keep its entrance
one woman living nearby worried about the wall she shares with her yard
the engineer promised shoring and then repointing at the builder's cost
a father raised the passing of trucks at the hour when children come home
text: The site manager presented the renovation plan to the residents who had come to hear him, and he arranged his answers around three worries. Noise came first. Demolishing the partitions would take two weeks, he said, and the noisiest machines would fall silent by late afternoon. Dust came next. A fine sheet would wrap the scaffolding, and the rubble would be dampened before it was carried out. Access came last. The sidewalk would be diverted around the works, though the shop on the ground floor would keep its own entrance. One woman asked what would become of the wall she shares with her yard. The engineer present promised it would be shored up and afterwards repointed, at the builder's expense. A father then raised the question of the trucks, and the hour when children walk home.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: lasting homes appear once groups stop moving from place to place
the first walls were branches packed with mud and made again after the rains
a silt paste hardened in the sun proved tougher than a fresh coating
the molded block could be made again exactly the same
a wall became a sum of matching pieces, which changed the builder's trade
firing in a kiln gave a block the rain could not touch
builders then grew bold enough to stack levels
the arch and then the vault freed openings from heavy timber crossbeams
every step forward rested on a repeated gesture and on a material taking over from the last
text: Homes built to last show up once a group stops wandering and decides to keep its stores in one place. The earliest walls were branches packed with mud, thrown up quickly and patched again after every rain. Then came the finding that changed everything: silt paste left to harden in the sun holds far better than a fresh coating, and a molded block can be made again and again exactly the same. From that point a wall was a sum of matching pieces, and the builder's trade shifted as much as the shape of the houses did. Later, firing in a kiln yielded a block the rain could not touch, and builders grew bold enough to stack one level on another. The arch, and after it the vault, freed openings from their heavy timber crossbeams. Every step forward rode on a gesture repeated and a material taking over from the last.

units: an inside wall can turn damp with no leak at all
the air of a heated home carries vapor given off by cooking, by showers and by breathing
the vapor turns to droplets when it meets a cold surface
cooled air holds less water than warm air
the cold spot usually comes from a local flaw in the insulation
the covering soaked with water ends up spread with dark stains
warming the surface by fixing the flaw takes the cause away
carrying the vapor off through steady ventilation also takes the cause away
drying the stain on its own settles nothing because the cold surface stays
text: An inside wall can go damp with no leak anywhere, and the physics behind it is well understood. The air in a heated home carries vapor, given off by cooking, by showers, and by the breathing of everyone inside. That vapor drifts freely until it meets a cold surface. There it turns to droplets, because cooled air holds less water than warm air does. The cold spot usually traces back to a flaw in the insulation: a concrete lintel, a badly protected corner, a window sill running clean through the wall. Moisture settles there, the covering drinks it up, and dark stains spread out over time. Two remedies reach the cause. Warm the surface by fixing the flaw, or carry the vapor away with ventilation that never stops. Wiping the stain dry changes nothing, since the cold spot stays put.

units: a property of three buildings ran into trouble while its roof was being redone
the firm stripped the covering off one wing before checking the frame
the inspection turned up rafters eaten hollow along their whole length
the work stopped
the temporary sheeting gave way in a downpour and water wrecked the ceilings on the top floor
the residents meeting in assembly refused to settle a second estimate
a mediator offered to share out the spending
the firm made the ceilings good at its own cost and the owners funded the replacement rafters
the house rules now call for an examination of the structure before any covering is stripped
text: A property of three buildings ran into an instructive mishap while its roof was being redone. The firm hired for the work stripped the covering off a whole wing before anyone checked the frame beneath, and the inspection turned up rafters eaten hollow along their entire length. Work stopped. The temporary sheeting gave way in a downpour, and water wrecked the ceilings on the top floor. Meeting in assembly, the residents refused to settle a second estimate. A mediator offered a way out. The firm would make the ceilings good at its own cost, and the owners together would fund the replacement rafters, which nobody could have foreseen in so old a structure. The deal held. The lesson now sits in the house rules: no covering comes off before the structure under it has been examined in full.
